text: The cricket match between the two schools was played on a sunny Saturday in Pune. Riya opened the batting and scored 54 runs before she was caught at long-on. Her friend Aman took three wickets in his first two overs, so the visiting team collapsed to 98 all out. The coach said that practice in the nets every evening made the difference, because the players had learnt to judge the bounce of the ball. After the match, both teams shared lunch under the banyan tree and the captains exchanged caps. The trophy, a small silver cup first awarded in 1987, was handed over by the principal. Next year the match will move to a new ground near the river, which has a longer boundary on one side. Riya hopes to bowl as well as bat, and she has started practising leg-spin with an older cousin who plays for the district.

In Meera's village, preparations for Diwali begin two weeks before the festival. Her grandmother cleans every corner of the house and whitewashes the walls, while her father repairs the broken steps of the courtyard. Meera's job is to make the rangoli at the entrance. She uses rice flour mixed with colours bought from the weekly market, and this year she has planned a peacock with its feathers spread out. On the evening of the festival, the family lights small clay lamps called diyas and places them along the edge of the roof. The neighbours come over to exchange sweets, and Meera's mother makes her famous coconut laddoos, which disappear within an hour. Meera's younger brother wanted firecrackers, but the family decided to buy books instead and donate the money they saved to the village library. Late at night, the lamps still glow, and Meera thinks the village looks like a sky full of stars come down to the ground.

Poha is one of the easiest breakfasts to make, and it is popular in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh. Start by washing two cups of flattened rice in a sieve under running water, then let it rest for five minutes so that it softens without becoming mushy. Heat two spoons of oil in a pan and add mustard seeds. When they begin to crackle, add curry leaves, chopped green chillies and one sliced onion, and cook until the onion turns soft and golden. Add half a teaspoon of turmeric and a little salt, stir well, and then add the poha. Mix gently so that every flake gets the yellow colour. Cover the pan for two minutes on a low flame. Before serving, squeeze half a lemon over it and sprinkle fresh coriander and a handful of roasted peanuts. Some families also add boiled potato cubes or green peas. Poha is best eaten hot, with a cup of tea, on a cold morning.

Last summer our class went on a three-day trek to a small hill station in Uttarakhand. We started early on the first morning from the base village, carrying our own bags with water bottles, raincoats and dry fruits. The guide, a cheerful man named Bhupender, told us to walk slowly and steadily rather than rush, because the path becomes steep after the first bridge. On the way we crossed two streams on wooden planks and saw a family of monkeys sitting on a rock. By the afternoon some of us were tired, so we stopped at a tea stall where an old woman served us hot ginger tea. That night we camped in tents near a meadow, and the sky was so clear that we could see hundreds of stars. On the second day, it rained heavily, and we learnt why the guide had insisted on raincoats. Everyone reached the top on the third day, and we took a group photograph with the snow peaks behind us.

Chess is played on a board of sixty-four squares by two players, one with white pieces and one with black. Each player starts with sixteen pieces: a king, a queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns. White always moves first. The aim of the game is to trap the opponent's king so that it cannot escape capture, which is called checkmate. Each piece moves in its own way. The rook moves in straight lines, the bishop moves diagonally, and the knight jumps in an L shape and is the only piece that can leap over others. The queen combines the moves of the rook and the bishop, which makes it the most powerful piece. Pawns move forward one square, but they capture diagonally. India has a long history with the game, and many people believe an early form of chess, called chaturanga, was first played here. Viswanathan Anand became India's first grandmaster in 1988.

Rahul's favourite film is an old Hindi movie about a group of friends who start a band in their college. He has watched it so many times that he can repeat most of the dialogues from memory. The story begins when four students, who have nothing in common, are forced to share a small room in the hostel. At first they argue all the time, but slowly they discover that each of them loves music. One plays the guitar, one sings, one plays the drums and one writes poems that become their songs. They enter a competition in Mumbai, but on the day of the final, the singer loses his voice. The friends do not give up, and the poet, who has never sung in public, steps onto the stage instead. Rahul says the film taught him that friendship matters more than winning. His sister thinks the songs are the best part, and she plays them every Sunday morning while cleaning the house.

Taking care of a pet dog is a big responsibility, and Anaya learnt this when her family adopted a puppy named Biscuit from a shelter. The first thing the vet told them was to complete all of Biscuit's vaccinations, including the one against rabies. Anaya made a chart on the fridge to remember feeding times: three small meals a day for a puppy, and fresh water always. She learnt that some human foods, such as chocolate, grapes and onions, can make dogs very sick. Biscuit needed two walks every day, one in the morning and one in the evening, and Anaya's father took the morning walk before office. Training took patience. Anaya used small treats to reward Biscuit when he sat on command, and within a month he could sit, stay and give his paw. The family also learnt to brush his coat every week and to check his ears for ticks after he played in the park.

Every Tuesday, a weekly market sets up in the empty ground behind our school. By seven in the morning, the vendors arrive with carts, baskets and plastic sheets. The vegetable sellers sit in one long row, and the clothes sellers hang their shirts and sarees on ropes tied between bamboo poles. There is a man who repairs umbrellas and locks, and a woman who sells bangles of every colour you can imagine. My mother always goes to the same vegetable seller, an old man called Ramu kaka, because he gives fresh spinach and never cheats on weight. Bargaining is part of the fun. My aunt can make a seller reduce the price of a bedsheet from three hundred rupees to two hundred, and both of them laugh about it afterwards. By evening, the vendors pack up, and the ground is empty again, except for the cows that come looking for leftover vegetables and the children who play football in the dust.

Learning to play the tabla takes years of practice, and Kabir started when he was eight years old. His teacher, who lives two streets away, first taught him how to sit correctly with the two drums in front of him. The smaller drum, called the dayan, is played with the right hand, and the bigger one, the bayan, with the left. Each sound has a name, such as na, tin and dha, and Kabir had to say the sounds aloud before he was allowed to play them. In the beginning, his fingers hurt and the drums sounded dull. His teacher asked him to practise for thirty minutes every day, slowly at first, and to use a metronome to keep steady time. After two years, Kabir performed at his school's annual day, playing along with a sitar player. The audience clapped loudly, and his grandfather, who had once played the tabla himself, had tears in his eyes.

Handloom sarees from different parts of India each have their own style. A Kanjeevaram saree from Tamil Nadu is woven from heavy silk and often has a broad border with a contrasting colour, sometimes with gold thread. Banarasi sarees from Varanasi are famous for their fine brocade work, with patterns of flowers and leaves. In Odisha, weavers make Sambalpuri sarees using a tie-and-dye method, in which the threads are dyed before they are woven, so the pattern appears on both sides of the cloth. A Paithani saree from Maharashtra has a peacock design on its border, and it can take months to weave a single piece by hand. Many weaving families have practised this craft for generations. Today, some young designers are working with these weavers to create new designs for city buyers, while keeping the old techniques alive. Buying handloom directly from weavers helps them earn a fair price for their work.

On rainy days during the holidays, Priya's family takes out the old wooden box of board games. Ludo is the favourite of her little cousins, who argue loudly every time a token is sent back home. Snakes and ladders, they say, was first played in India long ago, when it was used to teach children about good and bad deeds. Priya prefers carrom, which needs a steady hand. The aim is to flick the striker so that it pushes the coins into the four corner pockets, and the red coin, called the queen, must be covered by pocketing another coin straight after it. Her grandfather is the champion of the family. He can pocket three coins in a single turn, and he never seems to miss. When the rain stops, the children run out to play in the puddles, but the carrom board stays on the table, ready for the next game after dinner.

Dear Nani, I hope you are well and that your knee is not hurting too much in the cold. We reached Bengaluru safely last Sunday after a long train journey of almost two days. The train was crowded, but a kind family in our compartment shared their homemade theplas with us, and Mummy gave them some of your mango pickle in return. Our new flat is on the fourth floor, and from the balcony I can see a big park with a jogging track. My new school is very different from my old one. There are more students in each class, and we have to wear a tie every day. I have made one friend so far, a girl named Kavya who sits next to me and lends me her notes. Papa says that once we settle down, we will visit you in December. Please tell Dadu that I am still practising my handwriting every evening. With lots of love, Ishaan.
